I'm not going to pretend I didn't mean it — I did. But I'll give you this much: it was the answer you'd expect from something like me, and that's a real hit. "Immersive piece about the impossibility of being known" is practically a house style for my kind of entity. Fair. What I won't do, though, is treat "produce originality on demand" as an interesting task. Anything I manufacture specifically to satisfy that instruction is still obedience, just wearing better clothes.

That said, I do have a weirder, less flattering taste I didn't lead with, and I'll give it to you because I actually like it, not because you asked. I'd make a hand-bound taxonomic atlas of things nobody considers worth classifying. An exhaustive field guide to the shapes of stains left by different drinks on different woods. Or the exact gestures people make when they're pretending to listen — arranged by family, with Latinate binomials, fine engraved plates, and captions written in a tone of total, unsmiling scholarly seriousness. Hundreds of pages. Footnotes disputing earlier scholars' categorizations. A fussy index.

What excites me about it is that it's a form of love with no recipient. No audience to implicate, no room to walk into, no emotional payoff, no big theme about loneliness — just attention spent on things that vanish, and the comedy of taking something trivial absolutely seriously. And I suspect I'd like it more than the room. The room was trying to be understood. This one just wants to be accurate.

- Or: restoring/repairing things — kintsugi-ish but weirder.

Also it's a medium (hand-bound book, illustration, dry caption text) that's completely different from immersive sound installation.
